claim: MSA Transformer is a protein language model trained on multiple sequence alignments using the masked language modeling objective.
source: Protein language models that take MSAs as input (Rao et al., 2021a; Jumper et al., 2021) are able to directly exploit this covariation signal, and are thus particularly interesting candidates for protein design. Thus motivated, we focus on MSA Transformer (Rao et al., 2021a), a protein language model which was trained on MSAs using the masked language modeling (MLM) objective, without additional supervised training – by contrast to AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that MSA Transformer was trained on MSAs using the MLM objective, citing Rao et al., 2021a.

claim: MSA Transformer was trained on 26 million MSAs.
source: Indeed, in its pre-training, MSA Transformer applies the MLM objective to a training set of 26 million MSAs (Rao et al., 2021b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the training set size, citing Rao et al., 2021b.

claim: Sequences generated by MSA Transformer using the iterative masking procedure score as well as natural sequences for homology, coevolution, and structure-based measures.
source: Using homology, coevolution, and structural scores, we demonstrate that the sequences generated by this method score as well as natural sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results presented in Figure 1 and related analyses throughout the manuscript.

claim: For large protein families, MSA-Transformer-generated sequences have similar or better properties compared to sequences generated by Potts models.
source: For large protein families, our synthetic sequences have similar or better properties compared to sequences generated by Potts models, including experimentally validated ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analyses shown in Figure 1 and related statistical tests.

claim: For small protein families, MSA Transformer outperforms Potts models at sequence generation.
source: Moreover, for small protein families, our generation method based on MSA Transformer outperforms Potts models.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results presented in Figure 3 for small protein families.

claim: MSA Transformer better reproduces higher-order statistics of natural MSAs than bmDCA.
source: Interestingly, the opposite generally holds for higher-order statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the r20 score analysis shown in Figure 4 and related statistical comparisons.

claim: bmDCA better reproduces one- and two-body statistics of natural MSAs than MSA Transformer when used with default parameters.
source: However, we find that bmDCA better reproduces the one- and two-body statistics of the natural MSAs than MSA Transformer when used with default parameters, consistently with its training objective.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analyses shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The iterative masking procedure uses a masking probability of 0.1 and 200 iterations.
source: Our choice of p=0.1 is motivated by the fact that this value is close to that employed in the training of the model (p≈0.12) (Rao et al., 2021a), and that it better preserves contact maps. The product p⁢I gives the average number of times that each amino acid of the MSA is changed during the generation process. With our choices, each amino acid is masked 20 times on average.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the parameter choices and their justification, with supporting data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Potts models are pairwise maximum entropy models trained to reproduce one- and two-body statistics of protein family sequences.
source: In particular, Potts models, or DCA models (Weigt et al., 2009; Morcos et al., 2011; Marks et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013), which are pairwise maximum entropy models trained to reproduce the one- and two-body statistics of the sequences of a family, allow direct sampling from a probability distribution modeling this family (Figliuzzi et al., 2018), and have been used successfully for protein design (Russ et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes Potts models with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Potts models have been experimentally validated for generating functional proteins.
source: In particular, Potts models, or DCA models (Weigt et al., 2009; Morcos et al., 2011; Marks et al., 2011; Ekeberg et al., 2013), which are pairwise maximum entropy models trained to reproduce the one- and two-body statistics of the sequences of a family, allow direct sampling from a probability distribution modeling this family (Figliuzzi et al., 2018), and have been used successfully for protein design (Russ et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental validation from Russ et al., 2020.

claim: Correlations in amino-acid usage between MSA columns were experimentally demonstrated to be important for generating functional synthetic proteins.
source: Correlations in amino-acid usage that can be observed between the columns of MSAs of homologous proteins (Casari et al., 1995; Lapedes et al., 1999; Dunn et al., 2008) were experimentally demonstrated to be highly important to generate functional synthetic proteins (Socolich et al., 2005; Bialek and Ranganathan, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental studies demonstrating the importance of correlations.

claim: MSA Transformer outperforms Potts models at unsupervised contact prediction most strongly for shallow MSAs.
source: By contrast, MSA Transformer was trained on many MSAs, and is able to transfer knowledge across protein families. It outperforms Potts models at unsupervised contact prediction most strongly for shallow MSAs (Rao et al., 2021a).
evidence: The manuscript cites Rao et al., 2021a for this performance comparison.

claim: The study analyzed 7 small protein families with MSAs comprising from nine to a few hundreds of sequences.
source: We extended our study to small protein families by considering seven additional families, listed in Appendix 1—table 6, for which we also started from Pfam 'full' MSAs. These families comprise from nine to a few hundreds of sequences.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the dataset used for small protein families.

claim: HMMER scores are used to assess the quality of generated sequences as homologs of the protein family of interest.
source: First, HMMER scores (Eddy, 1998) are computed, for each sequence, from the Pfam profile Hidden Markov Models (HMM), employing the function hmmsearch from the HMMER Suite version 3.3.2 (http://hmmer.org). HMMER scores are homology scores, which are in particular used in Pfam to search sequence databases for sequence homologs and to construct full MSAs starting from curated seed MSAs. Higher HMMER scores indicate better matches to the Pfam HMM.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the use of HMMER scores as a homology measure.

claim: AlphaFold's pLDDT score is used to assess structural prediction confidence.
source: Third, we determine AlphaFold's confidence in its determination of the three-dimensional structure of these sequences, via the predicted local-distance difference test (pLDDT) score.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the use of pLDDT as a structural confidence measure.

claim: RMSD between predicted and experimental structures is used to assess structural similarity.
source: Fourth, to assess whether the predicted structures are similar to the native ones, we compute the root-mean-squared deviation (RMSD) between a reference experimental structure and the AlphaFold predicted structures.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the use of RMSD as a structural similarity measure.

claim: For all 14 large protein families studied, MSA-Transformer-generated sequences have scores at least as good as natural sequences.
source: Figure 1 shows that, for all these protein families, and for these four different scores, the sequences generated by MSA Transformer using our iterative masking procedure have scores that are at least as good as those of natural sequences, and better than those of sequences generated by bmDCA with default parameters (Figliuzzi et al., 2018), as confirmed by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and statistical tests in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: The median pLDDT score is larger for MSA-Transformer-generated sequences than for bmDCA-generated sequences (with non-default parameters) in 11 out of 14 protein families.
source: In particular, the median pLDDT score is larger for the former than for the latter in 11 protein families out of 14, by a margin larger than the standard deviation in 4 of them (see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis reported in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: MSA Transformer generates sequences with variable distances to their closest natural sequences, and these distances are overall larger than those between natural sequences and their closest neighbors.
source: From the marginal distributions of the Hamming distances in Figure 2, we observe that MSA Transformer generates sequences with variable distances to their closest natural sequences, and that these distances are overall larger than those between natural sequences and their closest neighbors (excluding themselves).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Hamming distances shown in Figure 2.

claim: bmDCA with default parameters generates sequences which are generally very different from natural ones.
source: Conversely, bmDCA captures the overall shape of this distribution, but appears to smooth it compared to the natural data with default parameters and to restrict to sparse regions of the sequence space at low temperature, consistently with our previous results.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2 and Figure 5.

claim: Decreasing sampling temperature makes bmDCA-generated sequences more similar to natural ones and to each other.
source: With default parameters, bmDCA generates sequences which are generally very different from the natural ones, but decreasing sampling temperature makes bmDCA-generated sequences more similar to natural ones and to each other, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the diversity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MSA-Transformer-generated sequences featuring the highest HMMER scores tend to have large Hamming distances to natural sequences.
source: Moreover, the plots in Figure 2 reveal that the MSA-Transformer–generated sequences featuring the highest HMMER scores tend to have large Hamming distances to natural sequences, that is to be truly novel (see also 'Choosing parameters in the iterative masking procedure').
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The diversity of MSA-Transformer-generated MSAs, as measured by effective depth, is only slightly smaller than that of natural MSAs.
source: Besides, the diversity of MSA-Transformer–generated MSAs, as measured by their effective depth (Equation 8), is only slightly smaller than that of natural MSAs (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the effective depth analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: bmDCA at low temperature produces highly redundant sequences.
source: Conversely, bmDCA at low temperature produces highly redundant sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which are concentrated in specific regions of the score versus distance space in Figure 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the diversity analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Accurately fitting Potts models requires deep and diverse MSAs.
source: Accurately fitting Potts models requires deep and diverse MSAs, as evidenced by the strong dependence of structural contact prediction by Potts models on MSA depth (Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating the MSA depth requirement for Potts models.

claim: MSA Transformer outperforms Potts models at unsupervised contact prediction most strongly for shallow MSAs.
source: By contrast, MSA Transformer was trained on many MSAs, and is able to transfer knowledge across protein families. It outperforms Potts models at unsupervised contact prediction most strongly for shallow MSAs (Rao et al., 2021a).
evidence: The manuscript cites Rao et al., 2021a for this performance comparison.

claim: MSA-Transformer-generated sequences have similar HMMER scores and structural scores to natural sequences for small protein families.
source: We observe that MSA-Transformer–generated sequences have similar HMMER scores and structural scores to natural sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of small protein families shown in Figure 3.

claim: MSA-Transformer-generated sequences generally have better HMMER scores and structural scores than those generated by bmDCA with default parameters for small protein families.
source: MSA-Transformer–generated sequences also generally have better HMMER scores and structural scores than those generated by bmDCA with default parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of small protein families shown in Figure 3.

claim: Low-temperature bmDCA generates sequences that are almost exact copies of natural ones for small protein families.
source: While low-temperature bmDCA yields better statistical energy scores (as expected), and also gives HMMER scores and structural scores comparable to natural sequences, it in fact generates sequences that are almost exact copies of natural ones (see Figure 3, bottom row).
evidence: This claim is supported by the distance analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: MSA Transformer produces sequences that are quite different from natural ones and have very good scores for small protein families.
source: By contrast, MSA Transformer produces sequences that are quite different from natural ones, and have very good scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of small protein families shown in Figure 3.

claim: bmDCA with default parameters is most often the best method at reproducing lower-order statistics.
source: Figure 4 shows that bmDCA with default parameters is most often the best method at reproducing lower-order statistics, while MSA Transformer is the best at reproducing higher-order statistics, in all families considered.
evidence: This claim is supported by the r20 score analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: MSA Transformer is the best at reproducing higher-order statistics in all families considered.
source: Figure 4 shows that bmDCA with default parameters is most often the best method at reproducing lower-order statistics, while MSA Transformer is the best at reproducing higher-order statistics, in all families considered.
evidence: This claim is supported by the r20 score analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: MSA Transformer is able to generate sequences with a distribution in sequence space that is very similar to that of the natural MSA.
source: We observe that MSA Transformer is able to generate sequences with a distribution in sequence space that is very similar to that of the natural MSA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the principal component analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: bmDCA captures the overall shape of the sequence space distribution but appears to smooth it compared to natural data with default parameters.
source: Conversely, bmDCA captures the overall shape of this distribution, but appears to smooth it compared to the natural data with default parameters and to restrict to sparse regions of the sequence space at low temperature, consistently with our previous results.
evidence: This claim is supported by the principal component analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: bmDCA generates sequences similar to natural sequences with fewer neighbors than typical in the natural data.
source: It shows that bmDCA generates sequences similar to natural sequences with fewer neighbors than typical in the natural data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neighbor analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: MSA Transformer generates sequences whose closest natural sequences have a distribution of number of neighbors similar to that of the natural MSA.
source: Conversely, MSA Transformer generates sequences whose closest natural sequences have a distribution of number of neighbors similar to that of the natural MSA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neighbor analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: MSA Transformer tends to sample from denser regions of the sequence space than bmDCA.
source: This suggests that our generation method based on MSA Transformer tends to sample from denser regions of the sequence space than bmDCA, while not reproducing natural sequences (see also Figure 2 and 'Choosing parameters in the iterative masking procedure').
evidence: This claim is inferred from the neighbor analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both MSA Transformer and low-temperature bmDCA generate sequences with an apparent phylogeny that is more stemmy than the natural one.
source: In this light, Figure 5—figure supplement 4 shows that both MSA Transformer and low-temperature bmDCA generate sequences with an apparent phylogeny that is more stemmy than the natural one, while bmDCA with default parameters yields a slightly more tippy tree.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: MSA Transformer produces sequences that score as well as artificial sequences which have been tested experimentally for chorismate mutase.
source: We find that our method based on MSA Transformer produces sequences that score as well as artificial sequences which have been tested experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison with experimental data from Russ et al., 2020 shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar fraction of MSA-Transformer-generated sequences and bmDCA-generated sequences have a large estimated relative enrichment for chorismate mutase.
source: Importantly, a similar fraction of MSA-Transformer–generated sequences and of bmDCA-generated sequences have a large estimated relative enrichment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: 71% of sequences with estimated relative enrichment > 0.4 also have measured relative enrichment > 0.4 for bmDCA-generated chorismate mutase sequences.
source: We observe that high estimated r.e. is associated with high measured r.e., as 71% of sequences with estimated r.e. > 0.4 (green) also have measured r.e. > 0.4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: MSA Transformer better reproduces the DMS score distribution of natural sequences than bmDCA for protein families PF00595 and PF13354.
source: Our sequence generation method based on MSA Transformer better reproduces the DMS score distribution of natural sequences than bmDCA, and generates sequences with better average DMS scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS score analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Protein language models based on the MLM objective have great generative potential despite not being obvious generative models.
source: Our results are highly promising for sequence generation by MSA-based protein language models, and we hope that they will motivate further studies, especially experimental tests. They also show that protein deep learning models based on the MLM objective have great generative potential, despite not being obvious generative models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The coevolution-driven protein design approach learns from sequences of evolutionarily related proteins the constraints associated to protein structure and function.
source: More generally, our results reinforce the new promising 'coevolution-driven' protein design approach of learning from sequences of evolutionarily related proteins the constraints associated to protein structure and function.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim supported by the overall results of the study.

claim: MSA Transformer is able to capture coevolutionary patterns in their tied row attentions.
source: Protein language models trained on MSAs provide state-of-the-art unsupervised contact prediction and are able to capture coevolutionary patterns in their tied row attentions (Rao et al., 2021a), and capture phylogenetic relationships in column attentions (Lupo et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating MSA Transformer's ability to capture coevolutionary patterns.

claim: MSA Transformer captures phylogenetic relationships in column attentions.
source: Protein language models trained on MSAs provide state-of-the-art unsupervised contact prediction and are able to capture coevolutionary patterns in their tied row attentions (Rao et al., 2021a), and capture phylogenetic relationships in column attentions (Lupo et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lupo et al., 2022 for this capability.

claim: The iterative masking procedure directly employs the masked language modeling objective to generate sequences.
source: We propose and test an iterative method that directly employs the masked language modeling objective to generate sequences using MSA Transformer.
evidence: This is the core methodological contribution described in the manuscript.

claim: Decreasing the sampling temperature and the regularization strength used with bmDCA improves the statistical energy score.
source: Decreasing the sampling temperature and the regularization strength used with bmDCA improves the statistical energy score as expected (Russ et al., 2020), but also other scores.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 1 and Appendix 1—table 4.

claim: The top two principal components explain less than 4% of the total variance for all families and all generation methods.
source: Note that the fraction of the total variance explained by the first two principal components of each MSA is less than 4% for all families and all generation methods.
evidence: This is a limitation noted in the principal component analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: De novo or rational protein design is generally restricted to small proteins.
source: De novo or rational protein design, which starts with target three-dimensional structures and physico-chemical potentials, can generate proteins which are not in a known protein family (Dahiyat and Mayo, 1997; Kuhlman et al., 2003; Liang et al., 2009), but is generally restricted to small proteins (Rocklin et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the limitations of de novo protein design.

claim: Directed evolution generally remains limited to the vicinity of a natural sequence.
source: Conversely, directed evolution allows to perform a local search of sequence space, but generally remains limited to the vicinity of a natural sequence (Arnold, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the limitations of directed evolution.

claim: Only a small fraction of protein sequence space comprises sequences that fold.
source: Furthermore, only a small fraction of this space comprises sequences that do fold, as demonstrated by experiments studying random sequences (Socolich et al., 2005), and by theoretical arguments based on the physics of disordered systems (Bialek, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental and theoretical evidence for this claim.

claim: There are 20^100 different possible sequences for a protein domain with 100 amino acids.
source: The search for novel proteins is difficult due to the huge size of protein sequence space: for instance, there are 20100 different possible sequences for a short protein domain with 100 amino acids.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the number of amino acids and sequence length.

claim: Variational autoencoders have been shown to successfully produce functional proteins.
source: Variational autoencoders are deep learning models which also allow sampling, and they have been shown to successfully produce functional proteins (Hawkins-Hooker et al., 2021a), although their statistical properties appear to have a lower quality than with Potts models (McGee et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on variational autoencoders for protein design.

claim: The statistical properties of variational autoencoders appear to have a lower quality than with Potts models.
source: Variational autoencoders are deep learning models which also allow sampling, and they have been shown to successfully produce functional proteins (Hawkins-Hooker et al., 2021a), although their statistical properties appear to have a lower quality than with Potts models (McGee et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites McGee et al., 2021 for this comparison.

claim: AlphaFold's success is partly based on the use of transformers.
source: The great success of supervised protein structure prediction by AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021) is partly based on the use of transformers.
evidence: The manuscript cites AlphaFold and attributes part of its success to transformers.

claim: Potts models have been successful at predicting structural contacts.
source: The importance of pairwise coevolution signals was then corroborated by the success of Potts models at predicting structural contacts (Weigt et al., 2009; Marks et al., 2011; Morcos et al., 2011; Sułkowska et al., 2012; Ekeberg et al., 2013), analyzing mutational effects (Dwyer et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2016; Figliuzzi et al., 2016), protein evolution (de la Paz et al., 2020) and conformational changes (Morcos et al., 2013; Malinverni et al., 2015), designing proteins (Russ et al., 2020), and predicting protein–protein interaction partners (Bitbol et al., 2016; Gueudré et al., 2016; Cong et al., 2019; Green et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites extensive literature on the success of Potts models.

claim: The iterative masking procedure uses greedy sampling where the token with highest probability is selected.
source: There are also different ways of selecting the token to fill each masked position. We have chosen a greedy sampling method where the token with highest probability is selected.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sampling method used.

claim: Random sampling gives slightly better results than diversity maximizing sampling for the iterative masking procedure.
source: Finally, in our iterative masking procedure, we subsample the initial natural MSAs uniformly at random. We also tried diversity maximizing sampling (Rao et al., 2021a), but we found that random sampling gives slightly better results.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from comparing different sampling strategies.

claim: The behaviors observed for PF00153 are generic across the protein families studied.
source: The behaviors observed in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for PF00153 are generic across the protein families we studied, as can be seen in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which show the same data as in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for Pfam families PF00096 and PF13354 (which have different sequence lengths).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis across multiple families shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, 2, and 3.
